article_text:
The latest edition of the Lyon Biennale strikes a particularly timely note as it interrogates the sense and reality of what we see before us and questions our own states of mind.

Synchronised gunfire welcomed me to Gerland, one of the Lyonnais districts grappling with drug-related conflicts and part of a city lately racked by student demonstrations and outbreaks of unrest. A woman’s wailing echoed as I walked through the gates of Les Grandes Locos, the repurposed industrial complex that is now one of Lyon’s most important cultural venues. Tethered to an earnest expansion of the ‘principles of poetic economy’ first developed in the 1960s by the artist, filmmaker and activist Robert Filliou, more than 118 artists have gathered for the 18th Lyon Biennale. Under the theme Passer d’un rêve à l’autre / To pass from one dream to another , directed by curator Catherine Nichols, they are questioning “What is inherited and owed, cared for and desired, made, exchanged, used up and passed on.”

Shifting from one style of perception to another, passageways – or traboules – connect all 11 venues of the biennale. In her curatorial engagement with Lyon’s long history of circulation, Nichols reflects on Walter Benjamin’s unfinished Arcades Project , where he “explored how material history and collective dreams become entangled, and how imagined futures that were never realised persist within the present.” To pass from one dream to another, as she explains in her essay, “involves a moment of awakening”.

The moment of my own awakening came as the gunshots began again. What I perceived as a restaging of violence was, in fact, a Māori ceremonial call of welcome. In The Usual Cries of Welcome (2026), Ashleigh Taupaki retraces the approach of Ngāti Hako members summoned before a rūnanga , or pan-tribal council, in 1879. Close by, Taupaki laid tree trunks cut into many halves in the gutter, arranged in the form of a fallen Kahikatea, the tallest indigenous tree in Aotearoa (the Māori term for New Zealand).

Still at Les Grandes Locos, from a distance, Luz Broto’s Put Oneself in the Place of the Other (2026) served as instruction before entering the building: “When you arrive, put your keys on the table. Take a set of keys that are not yours to go sleep in that house tonight.” As I moved to the other venues, passing through the river, I caught a glimpse of Monira Al Qadiri’s inflatable sculptures of molecules, BENZENE FLOATS, through the glass walls of the Musée des Confluences. I saw another Luz Broto billboard, shouting in bold serif, in French, this time at the Musée des Tissus et des Arts décoratifs. Somehow, I hoped to see non-textile works, or less of them. But, as predicted, textiles across different contexts, scales and colours hang at varying heights. Silks are blue and embroidered in gold. Jacquard is imprinted with data. Fraying rugs, colourful tapestries and other over- and underwhelming fabric installations. There are cotton hammocks commissioned from Lyon’s Armenian community by artist Lucia Kagramanyan, Oror. Women’s song for the future. (A cradle, a sanctuary) (2026). Evoking both womb and cradle, turning into intimate space for rest or, in my case, a nap. It was there that I began to question the earnestness, if not softness, of this biennale.

I think of the hammocks, chairs and interactive installations begging an audience to take a rest. Nichols asks, referring to Filliou’s poetical economy, “What if value were measured not by profit but by creativity and play, imagination and generosity?” But what happens when generosity overburdens itself and circles back into profit? Should we doubt the generosity offered to us, by way of translations, themes of healing, a diversified artist list, and so on and so forth, or should we remain comfortable eating it all up?

As if sounding an alarm, Robert Filliou’s handwritten project woke me. At MAC Lyon, where many of his works are on show, he writes “You wherever you are”. I found myself coasting through the exhibition as though navigating a traboule . Pausing to see several works, I stumbled upon an archival passage of photographs, garments, advertisements and essays that led me to Archana Hande’s rotating light sculpture Weaving light (2009–2023–2025). I also walked through unpicked, unravelled rugs by Ouassila Arras. There was Pol Taburet’s bronze sculpture Papa (2025), which bore traces of the fears and desires of the legendary figure Papa Tonnerre, and somewhere I saw a hole punched through a wall, leading to a tropical landscape. Some cats were encased, too, and birds? These works upheld contradicting, if not perplexing, material history. What is actually being cared for here? What is merely being used up?

Retracing my steps, I examined Yasmeen Al Daya’s Embrace (2024). A small unfired clay sculpture, vitrined and spotlit, all its sides reflected on glass. A human form shrunk to be held in one hand, crouched in a foetal position. The tiny work in front of me was apparently made amid – and I quote the wall text – “[the] humanitarian crisis and destruction in Gaza following the strikes and military operations carried out by the State of Israel after the Hamas-led attacks.” The work was a replica. Is this what curatorial generosity looks like? Can artistic gentleness flatten radical art as it pursues political correctness? When institutions sanitise violence and crisis, are they protecting their own economy? At the Institut d’art contemporain, Lebanon’s collapse is examined in Disappearance Is Not Death (2026) by Joyce Joumaa. Revolutionary figure Youssef Bey Karam, along with his beliefs, writings and exile, becomes the film’s focus as it questions connections between memory and crisis, sovereignty and self-determination.

Eventually, I went back to Les Grandes Locos. Eventually, I found the biennale’s rough, radical edges. Installations are massive and moving, gigantic and consuming: a well-thought-out, well-arranged, seamless curatorial cluster of chaos. There is an aftermath of a rave, long ropes suspended, balloons, newspapers, office workers, a hand, a fish, a bicycle, a billboard. A dream passing into a dream. I walked through a salon and eventually ended up in front of a leather jacket pinned with a dead butterfly. In front of it was Samuel Georgy’s film installation, Life Is Difficult (2026), where a crying man was being shaved bald. A mirror presented itself, and I began to understand what I was looking for: a wake-up call. Or, honestly, the exit.

Walking out of the gate, the same gunshots woke me from a fever dream, leaving me questioning whether it was better to drift into an altered state of mind. Biennales, after all, are not established to answer queries, so I left carrying more questions. Is this dream merely a curatorial anaesthetic, a way for institutions to avoid dealing with realities outside their doors? Or are we too deep in doom that all we can ever do is dream?

The 18th Lyon Biennale runs until 13 December

article_text:
If you were planning on catching the West Coast debut of the Hollywood Vampires ‘ documentary Thursday night at the Newport Beach Film Festival , be warned that Joe Perry will not be in the sold-out Lido Theater.

While info for the 8 p.m. showing of the Daniel E. Catullo III-helmed Unleashed Spirits: The Rise of the Hollywood Vampires promises a “Live Q&A following the screening with Director Daniel E. Catullo III and members of the Hollywood Vampires!,” the Aerosmith guitarist and Vampires co-founder said this afternoon that he can’t make it after all.

Related Stories

Get Your Wings, Again: Aerosmith Sets Pair Of Comeback Concerts At Hollywood Bowl

Taraji P. Henson Encourages Artists To ‘Knock Down’ Walls, Sarah Finn Celebrates Casting Community & More At 2026 Newport Beach Film Festival Honors

“For anyone that may be planning to attend the West Coast premiere of the Hollywood Vampires docufilm Unleashed Spirits: The Rise of the Hollywood Vampires at the Newport Film Festival, I’m sorry to say that with Aerosmith performing together for the first time in three years, and rehearsing diligently for our two upcoming shows at the Hollywood Bowl , it’s become clear that I won’t be able to break away to attend personally,” Perry posted on his social feeds.

View this post on Instagram

It’s disappointing for fans who hoped Perry would be there like he was for the flick’s Boston world premiere in September, but you can’t deny the 76-year old Rock’n’ Roll Hall of Famer has been busy. The WME-repped Perry and HV bandmates Alice Cooper , Johnny Depp and Tommy Henriksen are just off a two-month European tour, and have a new-ish live album of rock classics.

Watch on Deadline

Add to that, Perry and his fellow self-styled “Toxic Twin” Stephen Tyler and the rest of Aerosmith unveiled earlier this month they were truly back in the saddle for a two-night stint at the Hollywood Bowl .

Bookending Halloween, the October 29 and November 1 Live Nation shows will see the band joined by likes of Guns N’ Roses Slash and Duff McKagan (the latter a former HV touring member), the living members of Run DMC, Billy Idol, the Black Crowes, Alice in Chains’ Jerry Cantrell, Heart, Eric Church and more diving into Aerosmith’s five-decade-deep catalog.

No word if Aerosmith is planning a tour of its own afterwards, or take up another Las Vegas residency as they did from 2019-2022.

The Hollywood Vampires were originally formed in the 1970s as a drinking gang for Cooper, The Monkees’ Micky Dolenz, John Lennon , The Who’s Keith Moon and Harry Nilsson. With Cooper off the booze years ago and Lennon, Moon and Nilsson no longer with us, the latest version of the Vampires came together in 2012 via the OG shock rocker Cooper, Perry and Depp. Since their 2015 live debut on the Sunset Strip, the band has toured regularly, with guitarists Depp and Perry relieving Cooper on lead vocals for a couple of David Bowie and Johnny Thunders tunes each show.

article_text:
As soft music crooned through the halls of a softly lit, glittering Grand Palais in Paris Tuesday evening, VIPs trickled in for a private dinner hosted by the Prix Pictet as part of the Paris Photo fair, which opens to the public on November 12. Wandering through the fair’s aisles featuring 246 exhibitors this year, it was unsettling to imagine that just a three weeks ago, Art Basel Paris had to evacuate the very same venue. Booths were dismantled early, the night before protests planned for October 24. The fair’s closure two days sooner than planned was unprecedented and came as a shock to many, ultimately necessitating Art Basel to offer a 20 percent discount on booth fees to all exhibitors.

Though civil unrest in France has not returned to the fever pitch experienced in October, and the government has exerted some greater control over the situation, demonstrations are continuing here, in an effort to bring attention to rising costs of living and under-funded public schools. How then, are Paris Photo organizers and exhibitors navigating it all?

“We are, of course, watching the situation closely to see how things evolve,” Photo Paris director Florence Bourgeois told ARTnews . “At this stage there is nothing new to report, and nothing alarming. In fact, for two weeks the demonstrations have been taking place peacefully, and generally in the east of Paris. So we are not alarmed, and we remain vigilant so that we can respond if necessary.”

Bourgeois said that the fair has closed early once before, after the 2015 terror attacks in Paris; despite lacking appropriate insurance at the time, organizers reimbursed 20 percent of booth fees. “But that’s no indication of what might happen in 2026,” she said. “It was an extremely different situation to that of the current protests.” (She declined to comment further on the fair’s current insurance policy.)

“If we ever do face something along those lines, our decision would be made based on protecting everyone’s safety. That’s the priority,” she added.

For German gallerist Thomas Zander , who exhibited at the shortened Art Basel Paris and is now back for Paris Photo, the city is the biggest draw. “It’s strange in a way, but I love Paris,” he said, characterizing this year’s Art Basel Paris as inspiring a “difficult feeling” in him. The early closure cost him “two good days” of sales, he said, adding, “Now we are in a better situation this week, and there are not so many demonstrations in the center, and it’s quieter than the week of Art Basel Paris.”

At the fair, his booth has on view what he described as “museum-quality works” because “all the museum people come here, to Paris Photo.” This includes a set of six dye transfer unique master prints by William Eggleston from 1968 to 1973, priced together at €1 million ($1.11 million); a rare series of 41 vintage gelatin silver prints of pinball machines by Candida Höfer, which are being sold as a single display for €600,000 ($665,570); and 16 works from Zoe Leonard’s “Analogue” series (1998–2009) about New York’s changing Lower East Side and offered for a total of €140,000 ($155,300).

In terms of price point, Paris Photo is a much more accessible fair than Art Basel Paris, where artworks are frequently offered in the six-, seven-, and even eight-figures. While some exhibitors at Paris Photo might make a sale over $1 million, the prices for other works can start as low as a few hundred dollars, with artist-signed books even costing under $100.

Despite having lower prices than the markets for contemporary painting and sculpture, the photography market has not been immune to the rest of the cooling that the global art market has faced in the past few years, according to Bourgeois, who said that more than ever closing a sale “comes down to a question of quality, which is why we’ve worked hard to represent the best that photography has produced over the last 200 years.” Even still, “for top quality photographic works, prices remain high and are not falling,” she added.

Several dealers said that approachability and a perceived distancing from the billionaire’s club of collectors often plays to the favor of Paris Photo, as protestors demand greater social equality. (In October, there were calls to protest outside Art Basel Paris and “take back the Grand Palais” from the wealthy few.)

“By taking part in a fair, we are not ignoring the realities of life around us, nor disconnected from it,” Bourgeois said. “We also represent part of the economy: there are galleries that make a living from this, that represent artists, give them visibility and support them by selling their work. I believe all of this is very important.”

“I’ve been hearing from a lot of people that Paris Photo doesn’t have quite the same image as Art Basel,” Paris dealer Anne-Laure Buffard said. “It’s a fair that has less of a connotation symbolizing a certain concentration of wealth, or an elitism reserved for the extremely rich.” With the recent closure in mind in light of the protesters, which have calmed, Buffard said, “We’re all trying to stay optimistic.”

She is presenting salt-washed, crystalline photographs taken in the Dead Sea, on the border between Israel, Jordan, and the West Bank, by Ilanit Illouz, priced from about $2,000 to $17,750; as well as painted and drawn photographs by Vasantha Yogananthan chronicling the impact of tourism on the northern Indian region of the Himalayas, priced between about $3,300 and $11,100.

Elsewhere, Pace Gallery is offering a jewel of a 1926 vintage gelatin silver print on a treated postcard by André Kertész for $500,000. It is thought to be one of only six or seven in the world. On the more affordable end, medium-sized still life photographs by Kiki Smith have already sold for $8,500 apiece.

“It’s been a very strong first day, with a number of significant sales made in the first hours of the fair, reflecting the strong demand for photography,” Pace senior vice president Lauren Panzo said. “It’s particularly encouraging to see so many new collectors coming through” alongside existing clients.

On Tuesday evening, Panzo told ARTnews that while the gallery has considered the possibility of further interruptions to the fair from ongoing protests, she is “personally not concerned—there are always protests here,” and the current ones seem to be more “under control.” She expects that over the weekend there will be lines to get into the Grand Palais as there have been in years past. “People in Paris love photography. I think there’s such a love for this medium. It’s so accessible,” she said. “Photography is different.”

Greeting visitors upon entering the Grand Palais is a large installation of works spanning the career of German photographer Thomas Ruff, a collaboration by his five galleries: David Zwirner, Konrad Fischer, Mai 36, Lia Rumma, Sprüth Magers. Other highlights a selection spotlighting women photographers, who now make up 38 percent of artists represented at the fair, up from 20 percent when the program launched in 2018, and around 100 newly acquired and unseen photographs from the Centre Pompidou’s collection. The Prix Pictet also now has a dedicated booth, featuring works by this year’s winner: Valérie Belin’s Still Life , showing an accumulation of plastic goods and memento mori, and Alfredo Jaar’s The End , which documents the receding Great Salt Lake in Utah.

A curated selection of artworks spread throughout the Grand Palais represents every decade since the creation of photography, which is marking its 200th anniversary this year. On one end is Serge Plantureux, which has on view what is considered the world’s oldest known existing photograph, an original print of photography pioneer Joseph Nicéphore Niépce’s View from the Window at Le Gras (1825).

On the other end is an installation of works by Alessandro Calabrese in the booth of Milan’s Viasaterna gallery. Priced between $2,440 to $8,430, these dreamy works are made by printing images on the “wrong” side of glossy photo paper, resulting in painterly, electric-hued prints. “In the end, it creates a sort of watercolor painting, but [made] automatically,” Calabrese told ARTnews . “All my research is based on looking for the limit of the figurative side and the realism in photography, and trying to challenge it.”
excerpt_original: If faced with a similar scenario to the protests that forced Art Basel Paris to close early last month, "our decision would be made based on protecting everyone’s safety. That’s the priority,” said Paris Photo director Florence Bourgeois.

article_text:
Tom Cruise will receive the 52nd AFI Life Achievement Award , joining a past roster of honorees that includes Hollywood greats from Bette Davis and Gregory Peck to Meryl Streep and Francis Ford Coppola.

The American Film Institute Board of Trustees made the announcement today, calling the trophy “the highest honor for a career in film.” The award will be presented to Cruise at a Gala Tribute at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles on Saturday, April 24, 2027.

“Tom Cruise is a global icon,” said Kathleen Kennedy, Chair of the AFI Board of Trustees. “As an actor and producer, he brings an extraordinary commitment to everything he does. What I especially admire is his deep belief in movies and their ability to bring people together. That passion has made him an extraordinary ambassador for American film around the world. It is AFI’s honor to present him with the 52nd AFI Life Achievement Award.”

Related Stories

‘Digger’ Review: Tom Cruise Explodes In Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s Surprising And Urgent Disaster Movie Satire

Hollywood Heavyweights Turn Out To Support Tom Cruise & His New Movie ‘Digger’ – Photos

A three-time Oscar nominee whose films have earned nearly $13 billion in worldwide box office, Cruise counts an impressive roster of films among his credits: Risky Business, Top Gun, Jerry Maguire, A Few Good Men, the Mission: Impossible series and many more. He currently stars in Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger , a film that has polarized audiences even as it stands as one of the most talked-about movies of the season.

Watch on Deadline

Cruise is set to return as Cole Trickle in Days of Thunder 2 .

Cruise has previously been honored by the Cannes Film Festival, the Producer’s Guild of America, France’s Knight of the Legion of Honor, Harvard’s Hasty Pudding Man of the Year Award, the John Huston Award from the Artists Rights Foundation, the Simon Wiesenthal Humanitarian Award, the Entertainment Icon Award from the Friar’s Club, the Will Rogers Motion Picture Pioneers Foundation’s Pioneer Award. In 2025, Cruise received the Honorary Oscar at the Academy Award’s Governor’s Awards.

The most recent recipients of the AFI Life Achievement Award are Eddie Murphy, Francis Ford Coppola, Nicole Kidman, Julie Andrews, Denzel Washington, George Clooney and Diane Keaton. The award was first presented in 1973 to director John Ford.

article_text:
Skydance shares closed down 22% Wednesday to end the session at just over $7 after the company distributed warrants to investors. Apple shares rose but tech stocks and overall markets mostly ended in the red after a worse-than-expected September inflation reading sparked fears of higher interest rates that hit debt-heavy companies particularly hard.

Related Stories

Evan Shapiro Pegs Skydance Value At Only $29B As His Media Universe Map Updates

Who Is In Charge At Skydance International – For Now At Least

Apple saw its market capitalization cross the $5 trillion mark again, a level it first hit last July. The stock is up 26% year to date and nearly 40% over the past 12 months. It closed up 0.5% today at $343. New CEO John Ternus took over as CEO from Tim Cook on September 1 and investors are upbeat on the tech giant, which recently unveiled the foldable iPhone Duo. Apple and Nvidia are the only two companies ever to hit $5 trillion.

Other tech companies from Meta (-3.3%), Amazon and Alphabet (both down 1.7%), which are investing heavily in AI, to Snap (-6%) and Spotify (-0.6%) went in the opposite direction. Netflix shares drifted lower but ended the session up a hair (+0.16%). The streamer unveiled hefty job cuts earlier Wednesday.

Watch on Deadline

In the final step of its giant media merger, Skydance distributed one warrant to purchase one share of Class B common stock for each share held by a public stockholder as of the Oct. 5 record date. The company said today after market close that it had issued a total of about 471 million warrants to holders of about 9% of its common stock. The warrants began trading on the New York Stock Exchange today (separately from the stock) under the symbol SKYD.WS with an official closing price of $2.20.

The company had signaled last week ahead of the October 6 close of the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger that it would let public investors access the warrants. About 90% of the investor base of the company, including Larry Ellison , the Oracle billionaire and father of Skydance CEO David Ellison, as well as RedBird Capital, Middle East sovereign wealth funds and other backers, did not receive the warrants.

Shares of Oracle fell about 9% amid a broader downturn for stocks of top AI stakeholders. Year to date, Oracle stock is down 33%.

The merged and renamed Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery had a rocky debut when it started trading under its new symbol, SKYD. The combined company has a massive debt load of nearly $80 billion. Rising interest rates can make debt harder to manage and Wall Streeters are wary of Skydance’s high leverage and ability to find a promised $6 billion in cost synergies.

Investors will be looking for strategic clarify from Skydance, Netflix and others as quarterly earnings season kicks off next week.

U.S. annual inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ latest Consumer Price Index. That was higher than anticipated as energy prices continued to spike, driven higher by the Trump administration’s war with Iran. Gas prices surged 34% year-over-year.

Rising inflation puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again after a hike in September.

The Nasdaq market fell by 1.9%, the Russell 2000 by 1.9%, and the S&P 500 shed 1.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost about 50 points. All ended the day off their lows.

article_text:
A sense of desperation is understandably in the air over at DC, the company, like Marvel, slowly realising that the mass superhero fever has finally broken. There’s still interest there, of course (this summer’s Spider-Man is now the biggest film of all time in the US after all), but it’s no longer good enough to leave a high-speed conveyor belt unmanned, purpose and quality control be damned. 2019 saw a staggering 10 superhero films released in cinemas, and the inevitable exhaustion that followed, also fueled by Covid, led to a gradual winding down, monster hits turning into minor ones and sure bets often becoming expensive flops.

As Peter Parker winged his way to box office records this summer, DC’s Supergirl bombed so hard that experts believe it might have cost Warners upwards of $200m in losses. It was just the latest disappointment for the brand after Black Adam, Joker: Folie à Deux, Blue Beetle and The Flash all underperformed while even last year’s much-heralded Superman reboot only grossed a solid $618m, a far cry from the $1bn heyday of the genre (things got so bad that even a fully filmed Batgirl adventure was deleted for the tax break ). Notably, the last DC film to swoop past that magic figure was Joker in 2019, a darker, lower-budget attempt to spotlight a villain rather than a hero, a big swing with relatively low stakes. Todd Phillips’s film might be best known by some for being brave enough to ask the question, “What if Taxi Driver sucked?” but for all of its many issues, it brought buzz and prestige and, shockingly, Oscars, to an easily ridiculed universe. It was also, crucially, something rare in that world: a close-to-good idea.

The evolution of Clayface, another R-rated villain origin story with a markedly lower budget than the DC norm, was not in direct response to Joker (it is allegedly the first in a new “Gods and Monsters” strand) but its path is one that head James Gunn would clearly like to emulate, albeit financially rather than awards-wise. One of many thoughts I had during Clayface, other than what I should have for dinner and how long I might be able to make a small popcorn last, was just how striking Phillips’s film stands in comparison. It remains shallow and smug and cursed with a grating lead performance, but it was visually punchy and, like the very best comic book adaptations, genuinely transporting, rich on dank atmosphere and thoughtfully curated production design. It was an undeniable moment.

Clayface is overwhelmingly not a moment. Admittedly its targets are way lower (Mike Flanagan’s original script, allegedly more texturally complex, was entirely rewritten ) but even as a similarly new way in, as a relatively standalone horror movie for those who wouldn’t now rush toward a superhero caper, it’s a clumsily missed opportunity and another reminder that those at DC don’t seem to know what they’re doing and why they’re doing it.

Rather than feeling like a lower-budget DC movie (it was made for around $40m), it looks closer to a network TV series, more Fox than HBO Max, more Gotham than Lanterns. With the standard there now so high (The Penguin looked every bit a blockbuster movie), the distractingly tinny aesthetic and lack of confident directorial style is disappointing both as a horror (especially at a time of micro-budgeted films such as Obsession and Backrooms looking so very distinctive) and as a tale that takes place in the DC universe. Liverpool was used as a stand-in here and if, like me, you found Manchester to be an unconvincing New York in Brand New Day, you won’t realise how good we had it …

Gotham is where working-class boy done good Matt (Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries, fine enough) is from and a place that he was desperate to leave. He’s a rising movie star, riding high after his first Oscar nomination (“Nominees don’t wait in line!”) and on a trip back to his home town, he makes the mistake of sleeping with the girlfriend of a violent gangster, introduced by Goldfrapp’s Ooh La La, one of the film’s many dated attempts at cool. As a result, he has his money-making face sliced up by goons and his career soon crumbles, back to a bedsit with all his money wasted on useless surgeries orchestrated by his viperous lawyer.

Matt is desperate for revenge and resurrection, and after stumbling upon a doctor working on experimental skin surgery (Naomi Ackie, trying her hardest), he thinks he’s found his chance. But before you can say Substance (the elixir is at least red here over Brat green), things go horribly wrong …

What the film does do is successfully gross us out, as Matt’s skin starts to morph in tune with his emotional state, which might be enough for some, and in the screening I attended, mostly filled with rowdy non-journalists, there was a vocal response to the goriest and gloopiest moments. The trailer scene, of Matt trying to cut through flesh growing over his eyes while on a bumpy flight, is brilliantly awful to watch, and it’s in these more intimate, uneasy moments where director James Watkins shows off his dusty genre mettle. His best films have been his earlier, smaller attempts – 2002’s genuinely creepy and forward-thinking reality TV horror My Little Eye and 2008’s brutal hoodie thriller Eden Lake – but he’s less assured when the canvas is expanded.

Clayface is as poorly lit and junkily made as the very blandest of streaming movies and never once do we feel transported to Gotham with a cast of exclusively non-American actors trying to out-accent each other (Eddie Marsan, as ever, loses that game). It doesn’t help that what could have been interesting at one point (perhaps when Flanagan was the sole author) with briefly pointed at issues of AI, unreality and method acting, has been sanded down to a kill-by-numbers revenge thriller led by a character who feels like an off-brand swirl of Venom, Hulk, Joker and Mystique. His abilities, and the rules of how they work, are so poorly defined, that he just becomes a screenwriting device, able to do whatever is needed in the moment.

Any tragedy that could and should have come from the character and his journey – boy from the wrong side of the tracks to privileged Oscar nominee to flesh-stretching, face-changing supervillain (!) – is excised for an easier video game trajectory, from one familiar level to the next (despite those involved comparing this to The Fly, this is very much not that). Clayface might be the start of a “bold” new era for DC’s superhero output but for anyone outside of a boardroom, it’s a face we have seen many times before.

Clayface is out in Australian cinemas on 22 October and in US and UK cinemas on 23 October

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "毕加索、安迪·沃霍尔和大卫·霍克尼都曾对腊肠犬倾倒。然而，这种性格顽固的狗狗远不止是一个缪斯：不来梅美术馆（Kunsthalle Bremen）的一场展览正展现了它身上所蕴含的无数讽刺、恶意与时代历史。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "巴勃罗·毕加索那只生于斯图加特的狗狗鲁姆普（Lump）倔强得无以复加，它原本属于摄影师大卫·道格拉斯·邓肯（David Douglas Duncan），但它却执意要留在这位西班牙画家身边。“当我拜访毕加索时，鲁姆皮跟着进来了，环顾四周：‘这就是我的——再见！’然后抛下我，去和毕加索生活了。”鲁姆普成为了这位出了名难以建立亲密关系的艺术家维持最久的伴侣关系之一，他反复为它作画、素描，其中包括他为委拉斯开兹的画作《宫娥》所作的研究，在这些研究中，仅鲁姆皮一人就出现了15次。毕加索比他的狗只多活了十天，顺便提一句，这只狗当时也正饱受脊椎疾病的折磨——这也是“畸形育种”话题的一个例证。", "links": [{"text": "Fotografen David Douglas Duncan", "url": "https://www.monopol-magazin.de/picasso-fotograf-david-douglas-duncan-mit-102-jahren-gestorben"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当毕加索看着它时，他眼中闪烁着一种温暖的温柔，非常短暂，几乎无法用相机捕捉，”邓肯回忆道，但他一次又一次地尝试，甚至出版了一整本关于毕加索与鲁姆普肖像的书。“他们是灵魂伴侣。毕加索是个独行者。一个按自己直线生活的人。鲁姆普也是。当你把它抱起来时，它会转过头去。我想它是喜欢我的。但它讨厌别人把它紧紧抱住。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "难怪毕加索在他那幅被无数次复制的素描《Le Chien》（狗）中描绘了一只腊肠犬，因为它就是那种原型的狗：完全按照人类的意愿塑造，却又充满固执的个性。一只拥有如此（艺术家般的）自我和如此长长脊背的动物，完全能够撑起一整场展览，因此不来梅美术馆为这个品种举办专属的艺术展便显得顺理成章。展览题为《腊肠犬：偶像出遛》（Der Dackel. Eine Ikone geht Gassi），自周末起展出约120件历史与当代作品。当然，帕布利托（Pablito）和鲁姆皮（Lumpito）也没有缺席，由慷慨的邓肯为其拍摄。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://monopol-prod.nbg1.your-objectstorage.com/s3fs-public/styles/max1560x1150/public/2026-10/David%20Douglas%20Duncan%20037.jpg?itok=8lMXoQOI", "alt": "黑白照片：坐在扶手椅上的老者，桌上有一只腊肠犬；前景中有一个模糊的人影。", "caption": "照片：明斯特毕加索艺术博物馆，© 德克萨斯大学奥斯汀分校哈里·兰森中心，大卫·道格拉斯·邓肯，毕加索让他的腊肠犬鲁姆普吃盘子里午餐剩下的食物，1957", "credit": "Monopol", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "安迪·沃霍尔也曾在宝丽来照片和丝网版画中一再记录他的腊肠犬阿奇（Archie）。皮埃尔·博纳尔、马克斯·利伯曼和罗丝玛丽·特罗克尔也无法抗拒下垂的长耳朵和小短腿所带来的美学吸引力。大卫·霍克尼则彻底着迷，他画下了他的腊肠犬斯坦利（Stanley）和布吉（Boogie）的各种姿态，当然，其中大部分都是它们在睡觉。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://monopol-prod.nbg1.your-objectstorage.com/s3fs-public/styles/max1560x1150/public/2026-10/Hockney_DogPainting46_95D08_0005_CC_23cm.jpg?itok=wCgASvRz", "alt": "大卫·霍克尼画作：两只腊肠犬在交叠的靠垫上休息。", "caption": "© 大卫·霍克尼。大卫·霍克尼基金会 大卫·霍克尼 《Dog Painting 46》，1995", "credit": "Monopol", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而，腊肠犬在艺术史中踱步时，并不仅限于充当其画家主人们的现实检验员，它身上还始终带着一种自我矮化的色彩，例如设计师奥特·艾舍（Otl Aicher）为1972年慕尼黑奥运会创作的标志和吉祥物：“瓦尔迪”（Waldi）同时也是对德国小市民习气的一种讽刺性象征，它强调了一个国家的无害性——就在不到40年前，该国还企图通过在柏林举办看似和谐的夏季奥运会来蒙蔽全世界。这就是瓦尔迪、阿奇博尔德（Archibald）和海德薇格（Hedwig）能够带给人们的教训：不要太轻易被腊肠犬无辜的眼神所欺骗，现实往往会以迅雷不及掩耳之势袭来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "芬兰艺术家埃琳娜·布鲁特斯（Elina Brotherus）的自画像同样充满了深渊感，画中她与自己的爱犬马尔切洛（Marcello）一同出镜，并竖起了中指，画作标题为：《我的狗比你丑陋的婴儿更可爱》。它是她系列作品《Annonciation》（2009-2013）的收官之作，该系列记录了她通过人工授精怀孕却终告失败的尝试。腊肠犬给人们的启示正是如此：必须宣泄挫败感，迷人的恶劣有时也是面对一个恶劣世界时唯一恰当的姿态。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://monopol-prod.nbg1.your-objectstorage.com/s3fs-public/styles/max1560x1150/public/2026-10/Brotherus_My-Dog-Is-Cuter_VG-BK_23cm.jpg?itok=mRn69-84", "alt": "埃琳娜·布鲁特斯，《My Dog Is Cuter》，彩色照片：一个人带着腊肠犬，在木墙前竖起中指。", "caption": "照片：路易Louisiana现代艺术博物馆，胡姆勒拜克，© VG Bild-Kunst，波恩 2026 埃琳娜·布鲁特斯 《My Dog is Cuter Than Your Ugly Baby》，2013", "credit": "Monopol", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Picasso, Warhol und Hockney waren dem Dackel verfallen. Doch der eigensinnige Hund ist weit mehr als eine Muse: Eine Ausstellung in der Kunsthalle Bremen zeigt, wie viel Ironie, Bosheit und Zeitgeschichte in ihm stecken kann"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Verstockt bis zum Gehtnichtmehr war Pablo Picassos in Stuttgart geborener Hund Lump, der eigentlich dem Fotografen David Douglas Duncan gehörte, aber darauf bestand, bei dem spanischen Maler zu bleiben. \"Als ich Picasso besuchte, kam Lumpi mit, sah sich um: Das ist meins – ciao! – und verließ mich, um mit Picasso zu leben.\" Lump wurde eine der längsten Beziehungen des bekanntermaßen bindungsunwilligen Künstlers, der ihn immer wieder malte und zeichnete, unter anderem in seinen Studien zu dem Velázquez-Gemälde \"Las Meninas\", in denen Lumpito allein 15 Mal auftaucht. article_text:
Picasso, Warhol und Hockney waren dem Dackel verfallen. Doch der eigensinnige Hund ist weit mehr als eine Muse: Eine Ausstellung in der Kunsthalle Bremen zeigt, wie viel Ironie, Bosheit und Zeitgeschichte in ihm stecken kann

Verstockt bis zum Gehtnichtmehr war Pablo Picassos in Stuttgart geborener Hund Lump, der eigentlich dem Fotografen David Douglas Duncan gehörte, aber darauf bestand, bei dem spanischen Maler zu bleiben. "Als ich Picasso besuchte, kam Lumpi mit, sah sich um: Das ist meins – ciao! – und verließ mich, um mit Picasso zu leben." Lump wurde eine der längsten Beziehungen des bekanntermaßen bindungsunwilligen Künstlers, der ihn immer wieder malte und zeichnete, unter anderem in seinen Studien zu dem Velázquez-Gemälde "Las Meninas", in denen Lumpito allein 15 Mal auftaucht. Picasso überlebte seinen Hund, der übrigens auch – Stichwort "Qualzucht" – an einer Wirbelsäulenerkrankung litt, nur um zehn Tage.

"Wenn Picasso ihn ansah, leuchtete eine warme Sanftmut in seinen Augen auf, ganz kurz, kaum mit der Kamera festzuhalten", erinnerte sich der Duncan, der es doch immer wieder versuchte und sogar ein ganzes Buch mit Picasso-Lumpi-Porträts veröffentlichte. "Sie waren seelenverwandt. Picasso war ein Einzelgänger. Einer, der sein Leben schnurgerade geht. Und Lump auch. Wenn man ihn aufhob, drehte er sich weg. Ich glaube, er mochte mich. Aber er konnte es nicht leiden, wenn man ihn festhielt."

Es ist kein Wunder, dass Picasso in seiner endlos reproduzierten Zeichnung "Le Chien" (der Hund) einen Dackel darstellte, denn er ist der archetypische Hund: ganz nach dem Willen des Menschen geformt und doch eigensinnig. Ein Tier mit solchem (Künstler-)Ego und solchen langen Rücken kann eine ganze Ausstellung tragen, weshab es unmittelbar einleuchtet, dass die Kunsthalle Bremen der Rasse eine eigene Kunstausstellung widmet. Unter dem Titel "Der Dackel. Eine Ikone geht Gassi" sind vom Wochendende an rund 120 historische und zeitgenössische Werke zu sehen. Natürlich sind auch Pablito und Lumpito dabei, fotografiert vom großzügigen Duncan.

Auch Andy Warhol hat seinen Dackel Archie immer wieder in Polaroids und Siebdrucken festgehalten. Pierre Bonnard, Max Liebermann und Rosemarie Trockel konnten der ästhetischen Anziehung von Schlappohren und Stummelbeinchen nicht widerstehen. Total obsessed war David Hockney, der seine Dackel Stanley and Boogie in allen möglichen Posen malte, vor allem schlafend natürlich.

Doch der Dackel dackelte durch die Kunstgeschichte nicht nur als Realitäts-Check seiner Malerherrchen, er hatte auch immer eine selbstverniedlichende Note, etwa in dem Logo und Maskottchen, das der Designer Otl Aicher für die Olympischen Spiele 1972 in München schuf: "Waldi" war auch ein ironisches Emblem zur deutschen Spießigkeit und betonte die Harmlosigkeit einer Nation, die nicht mal 40 Jahre zuvor mit nur scheinbar harmonischen Sommerspielen in Berlin die ganze Welt blenden wollte. Das ist die Lehre, die einem Waldi, Archibald und Hedwig mitgeben können: Lass dich nicht zu leicht täuschen vom Dackelblick, schnell schnappt die Wirklichkeit zu.

Abgründig auch das Selbstporträt der finnischen Künstlerin Elina Brotherus, das sie mit ihrem Hund Marcello und gerecktem Mittelfingen zeigt und dessen Titel lautet: "Mein Hund ist süßer als dein hässliches Baby". Es bildet den Schlusspunkt ihrer Serie "Annonciation" (2009-2013), mit dem sie ihre vergeblichen Versuche dokumentierte, auf dem Wege der künstlichen Befruchtung schwanger zu werden. Das lehren einem die Dackel: Frust muss raus, süße Boshaftigkeit ist auch manchmal die einzig angemessene Haltung einer boshaften Welt gegenüber.

Die Kunst der Woche in Bonn, Essen, Hamburg, Krefeld, Köln, Linz, New York, Potsdam und Wedel

Herlinde Koelbl in Bonn

Eine nackte Brust mit aufgemaltem Kreuz, ein Kopf unter einer Netzmaske mit einer Markierung: Die renommierte Fotografin Herlinde Koelbl hat 40 an Krebs erkrankte Menschen porträtiert. Die eindrucksvolle Ausstellung "Fadenkreuze für das Leben" im Kunstmuseum Bonn bietet einen künstlerischen Blick auf Krankheit, Verletzlichkeit und Hoffnung. Farbfotos zeigen in Nahaufnahme die markierte Körperstelle. Daneben hängen großformatige Schwarz-Weiß-Porträts und Tafeln mit Zitaten der erkrankten Personen. "Krebs ist ein Thema, über das man nicht gerne redet, obwohl es omnipräsent ist", sagte Koelbl.

Dass diese Menschen sich bereitgefunden hätten, sich mit ihrem entblößten Körper und in all ihrer Verletzlichkeit fotografieren zu lassen, mache das Besondere der Ausstellung aus. Dennoch sei es keine traurige, sondern eine mutmachende und lebensbejahende Schau. Ausgangspunkt sei ihre eigene Brustkrebserkrankung vor gut sechs Jahren gewesen. Für die Strahlentherapie seien die Bestrahlungsstellen auf ihrem Körper mit Fadenkreuzen markiert worden, schilderte die 87-Jährige. Dies habe sie an ihr früheres Werk "Targets" erinnert, für das sie weltweit Schießziele und Fadenkreuze des Militärs fotografiert hatte: "Dort dienten sie dem Töten, in der Krebstherapie dem Überleben."

Die Deutsche Krebsgesellschaft und die Stiftung Deutsche Krebshilfe sind Kooperationspartner des Kunstmuseums. In den vergangenen Jahren habe es große Fortschritte bei der Krebstherapie gegeben, sagte Mirjam Einecke-Renz von der Deutschen Krebsgesellschaft. Dennoch bedeute die Diagnose Krebs einen großen Einschnitt ins Leben. "Herlinde Koelbl trägt mit ihrer Kunst dazu bei, das Thema zu enttabuisieren und den Erfahrungen und Emotionen der Betroffenen Raum zu geben." Zum Rahmenprogramm der Ausstellung gehören unter anderem Vorträge von Medizinern und Erkrankten.

Koelbl zählt zu den bedeutendsten zeitgenössischen Fotografinnen in Deutschland und ist besonders für ihre Langzeitstudien bekannt, etwa über die frühere Bundeskanzlerin Angela Merkel (CDU). Für "Spuren der Macht" begleitete Koelbl über Jahre insgesamt 15 Persönlichkeiten aus Politik und Wirtschaft.

"Fadenkreuze für das Leben" , Kunstmuseum Bonn, Bonn, 8. November bis 16. Mai 2027

"Nach Damaskus..." in Essen

Noch vor dem Erwerb bedeutender Gemälde von Renoir oder van Gogh trug der Sammler und Mäzen Karl Ernst Osthaus (1874-1921), der zwei Museen gründete, Kunsthandwerk aus Nordafrika und Westasien zusammen. Osthaus bezog auch den aus der nordischen Mythologie stammenden Begriff "Folkwang" auf die Moderne, wo er für die Idee stand, Kunst und Leben sowie verschiedene Künste miteinander zu verbinden. Im Essener Folkwang Museum geben nun rund 300 Objekte – Keramik, Stoffe, ibero-islamische Fliesen – einen repräsentativen Überblick über die Sammlung islamischer Künste am Folkwang, die zu den frühen Museumssammlungen dieser Art in Deutschland gehörte. Werke der klassischen Moderne, europäisches Design sowie eine zeitgenössische Neuproduktion erweitern den historischen Blick um gegenwärtige Perspektiven und Fragestellungen.

"Nach Damaskus ... Karl Ernst Osthaus und die islamischen Künste" , Museum Folkwang, Essen, bis 21. Februar 2027

Affordable Art Fair in Hamburg Wer Kunst entdecken und vielleicht das erste eigene Werk mit nach Hause nehmen möchte, ist auf der Affordable Art Fair in Hamburg richtig. An diesem Wochenende präsentieren 90 Galerien aus 19 Ländern zeitgenössische Kunst zu Preisenzwischen 100 und 10.000 Euro. Neben etablierten Namen wie Gerhard Richter, Takashi Murakami und Katharina Grosse sind aufstrebende Positionen zu sehen. Neu ist ein eigenes Skulpturenareal. Im Eingangsbereich lädt außerdem eine begehbare Wasserinstallation des Berliner Künstlers Christian Kera Hinz dazu ein, Kunst nicht nur anzuschauen, sondern selbst Teil davon zu werden. Die Sonderausstellung "Common Ground" rückt drei Hamburger Nachwuchskünstlerinnen und ihre Auseinandersetzung mit dem Verhältnis von Mensch und Natur in den Fokus. Kostenlose Führungen und eine Wand mit Werken unter 1000 Euro erleichtern den Einstieg ins Sammeln.

Affordable Art Fair , Hamburg, bis 8. November

Art Cologne in Köln

Bei der Art Cologne stellen bis Sonntag 164 Galerien und Kunsthändler aus 22 Ländern aus – und hoffen auf gute Verkäufe. Die Spanne reicht von einigen tausend Euro bis hin zu Millionenbeträgen etwa für Werke des Malers Ernst Ludwig Kirchner oder der im August gestorbenen japanischen Künstlerin Yayoi Kusama. Die Kunstmesse kooperiert in diesem Jahr mit der Kölner Museumsnacht. Messebesucher können am Samstag die teilnehmenden 13 Museen besuchen – umgekehrt können Ticketinhaber der Museumsnacht die Art Cologne entdecken. Unsere Highlights finden Sie hier . Dazu gehört auch die Parallelausstellung "Circumspectio" : Anlässlich der Art Cologne wandern großformatige fotografische und grafische Darstellungen von Skulpturen von Heinz Breloh (1940–2001) in den öffentlichen Raum rund um den Bahnhof Köln Messe/Deutz. Breloh verstand Bildhauerei als körperlichen Prozess: Seine Bewegungen und die Auseinandersetzung mit dem Material schrieben sich in die Form der Werke ein. Die Schau greift diesen Gedanken auf und verteilt unterschiedliche Ansichten der Skulpturen über Passagen, Treppenaufgänge, Bahnsteige und Bahnhofsvorplatz.

"Art Cologne" und "Circumspectio" , Köln, bis 8. November

Slavs and Tatars in Krefeld

Parallel zur Ausstellung "Kunst Hand Werk Brücke" im Krefelder Haus Lange zeigt das Haus Esters eine vom Kollektiv Slavs and Tatars kuratierte Schau. Obwohl das Schaffen der Brücke-Expressionisten wie Kirchner oder Schmidt-Rottluff und die Praxis von Slavs and Tatars 100 Jahre auseinanderliegen, finden sich enge inhaltliche Verbindungen zwischen den Kollektiven. Gemeinsam mit weiteren Kunstschaffenden, darunter Egana Djabbarova und Nadia Markiewicz, erforschen Slavs and Tatars das Handwerk als Träger kollektiver kultureller und sozialer Bedeutung, um die oft übersehene Verbindung von Arbeit und Sexualität innerhalb gängiger Vorstellungen von Arbeit und der Erschaffung des Selbst neu zu untersuchen.

"Slavs and Tatars: Handdschob" , Haus Esters, Krefeld, bis 7. März 2027

Katrin Pla­včak in Linz

Die fröhliche Farbigkeit in den Malereien der 1970 in Gütersloh geborenen Katrin Plavčak kann nicht ablenken von der Ernsthaftigkeit, mit der die Künstlerin wissenschaftliche, gesellschaftliche und politische Themen verhandelt. Ihre Soloschau im Lentos Kunstmuseum Linz reflektiert das Leben und Malen in stürmischen Zeiten und hinterfragt, wie wir die Welt zwischen Fake News, instabilen politischen Verhältnissen und drohenden Krisen betrachten. Plavčaks Werke provozieren kritische Blicke auf geopolitische Gewalt, reflektieren die Bedeutung von Demokratie, beschäftigen sich mit Geschlechterrollen oder tauchen in reale Geisterwelten ab.

Katrin Plavčak "Pain­ting Rea­li­ty in Sur­re­al Times" , Lentos Kunstmuseum, Linz, bis 10. Januar 2027

Teresa Margolles in New York

Dass die mexikanische Künstlerin Teresa Margolles eine Ausbildung als Gerichtsmedizinerin absolviert hat, ist in ihren Werken unübersehbar. Seit fast vier Jahrzehnten setzt sie sich mit den Auswirkungen von Gewalt auseinander, insbesondere an der Grenze zwischen den USA und Mexiko. Ihre Arbeiten thematisieren Femizide, politische Vertreibung oder gesellschaftliche Vernachlässigung. Im Mittelpunkt ihrer ersten großen Museumsausstellung in den USA, die im New Yorker MoMA PS1 stattfindet, steht eine monumentale Barriere aus verdichtetem Schutt, den die Künstlerin aus einem verlassenen Haus in Ciudad Juárez abgetragen hat. Neben diesem minimalistisch anmutenden Objekt sind weitere Werke zu sehen, die um Gewalt und Verlust kreisen.

Teresa Margolles "At the Scene" , MoMA PS1, New York, bis 8. Februar 2027

Impressionisten in Potsdam

Es gilt als Publikumsmagnet und feiert sein Jubiläum mit Leihgaben von Dutzenden Galerien und Privatpersonen weltweit: Zum zehnten Jahr des Bestehens öffnet im Potsdamer Museum Barberini die internationale Schau "Die Impressionisten. Monet, Morisot, Renoir und ihr Netzwerk". Einige der dort ausgestellten Werke sind demnach selten zu sehen. 95 Gemälde und Zeichnungen aus neun Ländern sind laut Barberini extra nach Potsdam gereist, unter anderem aus Frankreich, Israel, Japan, der Schweiz und den USA. Sie sollen zeigen, wie "aus einer Gruppe junger Künstlerinnen und Künstler, deren Malerei zunächst auf Ablehnung stieß, eine der bis heute populärsten Kunstrichtungen der Moderne" wurde.

Der Impressionismus - entstanden im 19. Jahrhundert - ist im Barberini Programm: Gegründet wurde das bekannte Museum von dem Kunstmäzen und Software-Milliardär Hasso Plattner. Er hat eine Sammlung französischer impressionistischer und postimpressionistischer Malerei aufgebaut, die 115 Werke umfasst. Seit 2020 bildet sie das Zentrum der Dauerausstellung. Mehr als drei Millionen Menschen haben das Museum seit seiner Gründung besucht.

Anlässlich des Jubiläums werden auch die Gemälde der Dauerausstellung auf neue Weise präsentiert: "10 Werke, 10 Räume, 10 Geschichten", erklärt Kuratorin Sterre Barentsen. Ausgangspunkt sei immer jeweils ein Bild aus der Sammlung von Hasso Plattner.

"Die Impressionisten. Monet, Morisot, Renoir und ihr Netzwerk" , Museum Barberini, Potsdam, 7. November bis 21. Februar 2027

Janosch-Ausstellung in Wedel

Tiger, Bär und Tigerente: Mit diesen Figuren hat Janosch sein Publikum begeistert. Im Barlach-Kunstmuseum in Wedel (Kreis Pinneberg) läuft noch bis zum 4. April nächsten Jahres eine Ausstellung, die dem am Dienstag im Alter von 95 Jahren gestorbenen Schriftsteller und Illustrator gewidmet ist.

Der Titel der Ende Oktober eröffneten Ausstellung lautet "Janosch - Die Erfindung der Freundschaft". In einer Mitteilung des Museums heißt es: "Diese Ausstellung versteht sein Werk als einen großen künstlerischen Entwurf menschlichen Zusammenlebens. In den 235 Bildern begegnen uns Freundschaft, Liebe, Fürsorge, Freiheit, die Sehnsucht nach Glück und die Hoffnung auf eine friedlichere Welt."

Mit dem Tod des Künstlers, der mit liebevoll illustrierten Büchern wie "Oh wie schön ist Panama" seit den 1970er-Jahren nicht nur Kindern in aller Welt große Freude bereitet hat, bekomme die Ausstellung in Wedel eine neue Bedeutung: "Sie wird zu einem Ort des Abschiednehmens von dem Künstler, der Generationen von Menschen begleitet und ihnen etwas geschenkt hat, das in seinen Bildern und Geschichten fortbesteht: die Zuversicht, dass das Leben trotz aller Widrigkeiten schön sein kann."

"Janosch: Die Erfindung der Freundschaft" , Barlach Kunstmuseum, Wedel, bis 4. April 2027

article_text:
Filme tem estreia prevista para 5 de maio de 2028.

O Instituto Xavier ganhou um novo professor. O ator irlandês Peter Claffey se juntou ao elenco do novo “ X-Men ” produzido pela Marvel . Ele vai interpretar Henry “Hank” McCoy, o Fera, segundo o site Knight Edge Media .

Claffey é conhecido atualmente pelo papel de Sor Duncan, o Alto, na série “O Cavaleiro dos Sete Reinos”. Seus outros créditos incluem filmes como “Pequenas Coisas Como Estas” e séries como “Vikings: Valhalla”. Antes da carreira artística, Claffey foi jogador de rúgbi na Irlanda.

Com isso, este será o terceiro ator diferente a interpretar o Fera nos cinemas. O primeiro foi Kelsey Grammer, que assumiu o papel em “X-Men: O Confronto Final” e retornou para pontas em “X-Men: Dias de um Futuro Esquecido” e “As Marvels”. Mais recentemente, Nicholas Hoult viveu um jovem Hank McCoy em “X-Men: Primeira Classe” e nos filmes subsequentes produzidos pela Fox.

Claffey se junta ao elenco que já conta com Sadie Sink como Jean Grey, Kit Connor como o Ciclope, Inde Navarrette como a Vampira, Maya Boyd como a Tempestade, Asa Germann como o Anjo e Christopher Abbott como Charles Xavier, o Professor X. Entre os vilões, Samara Weaving será Emma Frost, e Adam Driver interpreta Nathaniel Milbury, o Sr. Sinistro.

Jake Schreier assume a direção do novo “X-Men” após o sucesso de “Thunderbolts*”. O roteiro fica a cargo de Lee Sung Jin, que já trabalhou com Schreier na série “Beef”, e de Joanna Calo.

O novo “X-Men” tem estreia prevista para 5 de maio de 2028.

article_text:
⁠Jurandir Filho ⁠, ⁠ Rogério Montanare ⁠⁠ e ⁠ Fernanda Bermoltz ⁠ conversam sobre a terceira temporada de “ A Casa do Dragão “. Dessa vez a história mergulhou de vez na “ Dança dos Dragões “, a guerra civil que coloca Targaryen contra Targaryen e ameaça destruir Westeros. Neste podcast, relembramos os acontecimentos mais importantes, analisamos os novos episódios, as grandes batalhas, as alianças, traições e, claro, os dragões que transformam essa disputa pelo poder em uma das guerras mais destrutivas da história dos Sete Reinos. Será que a terceira temporada conseguiu levar “A Casa do Dragão” para outro nível? E como essa guerra prepara o caminho para o futuro que conhecemos em “Game of Thrones” ?

title_original: A Landmark Survey of Native Graphic Arts Defies Expectations
editorial_title_zh: 一项具有里程碑意义的原住民平面艺术展打破了人们的预期
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在目前正在纽约海报博物馆（Poster House）展出并持续至明年2月的“Designed to Be Red”展览中，工艺、平面艺术与雕塑之间的界限消融了。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "直至明年2月，纽约海报博物馆（Poster House）迎来了“Designed to Be Red”，这是一场具有里程碑意义的原住民平面艺术展。按机构惯例，此类展览通常会按年代顺序展开；但正如其策展人、原住民设计师布赖恩·约翰逊（Brian Johnson）所指出的，时间是一条吞食自己尾巴的蛇。", "links": [{"text": "Poster House", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/poster-house/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这场展览跨越了两个世纪以及60多个部落与民族，围绕五个主题展开：原住民之乐（Indigenous Joy）、创作主权（Creative Sovereignty）、抗议（Protest）、情况复杂（It’s Complicated）以及掠夺性营销（Extractive Marketing）。各个板块环绕着一个展厅，允许参观者从任意一端开始。据约翰逊称，最好从“快乐”开始，尽管就连该板块那些迷幻的核心作品——60年代的青年动荡震动了原住民土地，其规模惊人——也暗示着麻烦。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“抗议可以说是整个展厅的顶梁柱，”莫纳坎印第安民族（Monacan Indian Nation）公民约翰逊说道。约翰逊策划这场展览的部分目的，是为了纠正平面艺术的档案记录，其在历史记述中边缘化了原住民从业者，并在大众想象中留下了历史创伤。美国人肯定还记得那些广告，也看过那些电影：心碎的“酋长”、挑衅的公主和骄傲的战士，被荒诞的方言贬低为幼儿状态，并被剥夺了个性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“这一切背后的核心理念是多元性，”使用he/they代词的约翰逊说。“美洲印第安人和原住民并不是一个单一的整体。我们有权谈论自己并被看到，而不是让某种神话被强加给我们，或是被编织进美国的社会结构中。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "参展艺术家包括肯特·蒙克曼（Kent Monkman）、Onaman Collective（展出了他们为达科他输油管道抗议活动创作的原版海报）；曾在最新惠特尼双年展上亮相的安娜·苏拉哈拉基（Anna Tsouhlarakis）贡献了一条来自其“原住民向导项目”（Native Guide Project）的横幅，上面用黑体（Helvetica Bold）的权威语气写道：我真的很喜欢你尊重美洲印第安人权利的方式。然而，这场展览将平面艺术的概念扩展到了连其主办方海报博物馆（Poster House）所划定的界限之外。杰弗里·吉布森（Jeffrey Gibson）也出现在与露泽娜·希尔（Luzene Hill）、埃里克-保罗·里格（Eric-Paul Riege）和达娜·克拉克森（Dana Claxton）等艺术家的系列欢快合作中，他带来了一座名为《因为一旦你进入我的屋子，它就成了我们的屋子》（Because Once You Enter My House, It Becomes Our House，2020）的微型金字塔，该作品以现代圣路易斯附近古代原住民大都市卡霍基亚（Cahokia）的建筑为原型。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "工艺、视觉艺术、设计：托尼·贡耶（Tony Gonyea）借鉴16世纪中期哈德森诺休（Haudenosaunee）传统的陶瓷瓦姆帕姆（wampum）腰带该归于哪一类？埃拉·迈尔斯（Ella Myers）的立体陈列盒《纳瓦约染料图》（Navajo Dye Chart ）又当如何，顾名思义，它展示了大约40种植物及其在羊毛上呈现的颜色？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“人们假定或强加了一条存在于这些类别之间的墙，但一个人既可以是篮子编织工或地毯编织工，也可以从事平面设计。艺术与设计融入了一切，”约翰逊说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "请继续阅读约翰逊与《艺术新闻》（ARTnews）关于展览的起点、终点和下一站的对话。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那么，关于这个标题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我喜欢这个标题的双关语：“Red”和“read”。我把一个种族歧视的侮辱词直接拍在你的脸面上，但这些作品同时也旨在被阅读（read）、理解、消化和沉思。这就像“红权运动”（Red Power movement）或“美洲印第安人运动”（American Indian Movement）一样——夺回对我们极其神圣的东西，并在展览一开场就重拳出击。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在一个平面设计展中看到如此多的三维立体物件很不寻常。这里的考量是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贯穿整个展览的问题之一是，什么才算是一张海报。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对我而言，在原住民语境下，海报是通过排版、视觉语言或地方语言传达信息，并意在公开展示或表达的东西。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《纳瓦约染料图》（Navajo Dye Chart）展示了如何利用植物制作不同的颜色。这位艺术家在20世纪80年代制作过海报，但印刷使用的是酸性纸张，作品很快就退化了。现在虽然还留存有一些信件，但我想要的是最初的图表——那个能真正展示在哪里可以找到特定植物以及如何用它来制作颜色的实体物件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这就是主权：宣告“这些才是你们应该讨论的事情。”我们在设计史课堂上可不教这些。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IND_009.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "杰弗里·吉布森（生于1972年，密西西比乔克托族/切罗基族），《因为一旦你进入我的屋子，它就成了我们的屋子》（2020年），艺术家供图，图片由海报博物馆提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你如何看待艺术与设计教育中的这一鸿沟？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在学校里，我们被告知德国人包办了一切，设计始于包豪斯，事情就该如此：瑞士排版。包豪斯之后，人们来到耶鲁，在黑山学院（Black Mountain College）教书，然后这些理念传播到了克兰布鲁克（Cranbrook）、奥蒂斯（Otis）、加州艺术学院（CalArts）等学校。艺术教育深陷于包豪斯的巨大阴影之中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "[我是] Polymode 的合伙人。我们设计书籍和博物馆展览已有20年了。2020年，我们创办了一所学校——BIPOC设计史（BIPOC Design History）。我们关注那些被蓄意抹去、被排除在设计正统之外的有色人种。我们的学校提供关于美国黑人设计（Black design in America）、平面设计（Diseño Gráfico）、西南亚和北非（SWANA）课程以及“（重新）创造海龟岛”（(re)Creating Turtle Island）等课程——我们邀请设计师和研究人员向我们展示他们认为被遗漏的内容。", "links": [{"text": "Polymode", "url": "https://www.polymode.studio"}, {"text": "BIPOC Design History", "url": "https://nam02.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fbipocdesignhistory.com%2F&data=05%7C02%7Ctsolomon%40artnews.com%7C406de5146eb942f02c1008df2bc1bd3e%7Ce950f25546e44144a778a6ff4f557492%7C0%7C0%7C639277783292675001%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=1FQI4KwXJh3icO5FeVwY86LbSbWFWq2nglIQdI7V2lI%3D&reserved=0"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“阿尔卡特拉兹与抗议”这一板块进一步使艺术、物件与设计之间的区别变得复杂。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "1969年，美洲印第安人占领了旧金山湾外的阿尔卡特拉兹岛（Alcatraz Island），并一直坚守到1971年。他们发表了一份宣言，要求归还该岛。在此之前占领该岛的定居者将其弄得破败不堪。原住民意识到这里已不再被使用，于是实际上宣告：“我们要把它拿回来。”他们将这份公告写在了一张拉伸的野牛皮上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "切罗基族公民、平面设计师艾玛·瓦格纳（Emma Waggoner）找到了它。这张兽皮过去在——现在也仍然在——阿肯色州美国法警博物馆的馆藏中。瓦格纳和她的妻子开车去那里实地考察。她们联系了博物馆，尽管其工作人员起初并不确定是否愿意把它借给我们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当时我正在圣菲与一个档案馆合作，档案保管员说：“等一下，我认识他们，”然后拿起了电话。他给博物馆打电话说：“嘿，你们馆里有那张兽皮吗？对，有个叫布莱恩·约翰逊的原住民想从我们这儿把它弄走。”再次说明，人脉让一切成为可能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是一件关键展品，因为它提出了一个问题：为什么原住民非得遵循把[设计]印在纸上的传统？为什么我们需要在追逐野牛、横穿平原时，在马背后面绑上一台巨大的印刷机？我们可以把信息写在兽皮上并把它挂起来。而且你看：这里有排版和公共信息，这就是为什么这是展览中如此重要的一个时刻。它既充满讽刺，又同时无比真实。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从我刚听说其存在的美国法警博物馆，来到曼哈顿。改变展出空间是如何改变这件物品的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这里，它得以表达自我、展现存在并发出呐喊。它没有被隔离或被称作囚犯；在这里，它拥有了语境。它是一件神圣的物品吗？不是。它还在跟我们对话吗？是的。它是一件抗议物品，帮助原住民争取到了我们今天拥有的权利。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我很感激 Poster House 在展览完全布置好后，足够细心地关闭了火警警报器，让我能够在这个机构空间里静坐。我一次又一次地向每一件展品道谢，尤其是这一件。我真切地在这个房间的筹备过程中生活过，并且说：“非常感谢你们来到这里。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "就像这里的许多作品一样，它的署名是“失落姓名的设计者”（Designer Once Known）。在博物馆里，在墙面文本上看到“未知艺术家”（Unknown artist）更为常见。其中的细微差别是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们在标签上写下“失落姓名的设计者”，而博物馆通常会写“未知”。这两者并不一样。“未知”是一种耸肩。它是人类学式的。没法证明。无从知晓。但那是垃圾。制作那件物品或那件作品的人是为人所知的。他们是被爱着的。这个名字并没有从物品上掉落。它只是没有被珍视。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“失落姓名的设计者”说明某个人是真实存在的，它赋予了他们人性。有人知道是谁的手切了那块版、印了那幅画、给那条三角旗穿上了珠饰——他们的名字、他们的部族、是谁教他们的、他们的血统、他们是为谁制作的——所有这些细节。因此，当我把“失落姓名的设计者”写在墙上时，我并没有放弃这个名字。我用尊严填满了一个空间，并怀揣着最终有一天能够将其填补完整的希望。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IND_002.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "《归还吗？》（Give It Back?, 2023），由新红党（New Red Order）携手莱利·胡克（Riley Hooker）和迪伦·克兰西（Dylan Clancy）为女王区 Creative Time 推出的讽刺狂欢节“世界不公”（The World's UnFair）创作。这张海报引用了宣伟（Sherwin-Williams）1893年的“覆盖地球”（Cover the Earth）标志，该标志描绘了一个血红色的美洲原住民 caricatures 将油漆倒在地球上的形象。鼓励对土地归还有兴趣的观众拨打海报上的 800 电话。ROBERT FELICIANO", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“情况复杂”和“掠夺性营销”被塞在后面，有点视线不及的地方。参观者在那里会找到什么样的作品？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该展区的一件核心作品已经收录在海报之家的收藏中：温霍尔德·赖斯（Winold Reiss）的作品。作为一名在19世纪80年代末来到美国的德国移民，赖斯成为了哈莱姆文艺复兴时期的一位重要画家。他曾教亚伦·道格拉斯（Aaron Douglas）画画，他为阿兰·洛克（Alain Locke）、兰斯顿·休斯（Langston Hughes）和佐拉·尼尔·赫斯顿（Zora Neale Hurston）创作的肖像画曾在纽约大都会艺术博物馆的哈莱姆文艺复兴展上展出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他还痴迷于“牛仔与印第安人”的故事。他去了蒙大拿州的黑脚族保留地（Blackfeet Reservation）。在那里变得非常有名；他们很喜欢这个随性的德国家伙。他花钱请他们当模特，出钱请翻译，把他们画成他们本该被画出的样子——这与爱德华·柯蒂斯（Edward Curtis）截然相反。他画了 280 幅肖像。他了解他们的故事，当他去世时，他们将他的骨灰撒在了保留地上。他还把所有这些画都卖给了大北方铁路公司（Great Northern Railroad）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而大北方铁路公司——叮、叮、叮——把这些肖像变成了营销工具来推广其路线。公司将它们复制在扑克牌和名片上。钱没有一分流回保留地。他们的名字没有被使用。也没有征求他们的许可。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但与此同时，排版美极了。这就是矛盾所在。这张海报制作精美，然而它却参与了一个为谋取商业利益而掠夺原住民、土地和意象的系统。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "情况复杂。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "情况复杂。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "赖斯在保留地上开办了一个工作坊？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "度假的人们会来到蒙大拿州并画原住民。他们得到了报酬，但他们也被当作某种边角余料的马戏团表演来看待，被卷入“消亡种族”的神话中。这里面有些黏糊糊、说不清道不明的东西。为什么不直接与他们合作，或者让他们教你串珠、教你我们传统中的东西？不，相反，这是这种米开朗基罗风格的宏大工作室。再次体现了艺术教育的西方观念。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IND_087.jpg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "温霍尔德·赖斯（Winold Reiss，1886–1953），《帝国建造者/西方之星》（Empire Builder/Western Star），（1952），Poster House 永久馆藏。图片由 Poster House 提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个展览接下来要去哪里？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这不是一个穷尽一切的展览。我们绝无可能代表全部574个（联邦承认的）部族。那些未被承认的部族怎么办？那些被彻底抹去的部族怎么办？正因如此，我绝不是唯一能够发声并策办此展的人。这个展览需要去到像派恩里奇（Pine Ridge）或俄克拉荷马城那样的地方。无论它去往何处，我都希望深入挖掘当地的档案馆，并扩展展览以契合每一个空间。这里有大量的莱纳佩（Lenape）材料，你知道的，因为我们正身处他们的土地上。我希望看到它的人成为它的支点，让它对他们而言具有意义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如我们所知，设计在许多方向上都充满了困境，而这个展览是史无前例的。我们必须把它带到服务不足的地区。我需要让原住民青少年看到他们能够创造这些事物，看到他们理应占据这个空间。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Through next February, New York’s Poster House is home to “Designed to Be Red,” a milestone survey of Native graphic arts. By institutional convention, such a show would unfold chronologically; but as its curator, the Native designer Brian Johnson, notes, time is a snake swallowing its own tail.

The show spans two centuries and more than 60 tribes and nations, organized around five themes: Indigenous Joy, Creative Sovereignty, Protest, It’s Complicated, and Extractive Marketing. The sections wrap around a single gallery, allowing visitors to begin at either end. It’s best to start from Joy, according to Johnson, though even that section’s psychedelic centerpieces—the ‘60s youthquake swept Native land, spectacularly—suggest trouble.

“Protest is literally the backbone of the entire gallery,” said Johnson, who is a citizen of the Monacan Indian Nation. Johnson assembled this show in part to correct the graphics arts record, which has both marginalized Native practitioners in its annals and left a legacy wound in the popular imagination. Americans surely remember the advertisements and have seen the movies: the heartbroken ‘Chief’, provocative princess, and proud warrior, infantilized by pidgin and hollowed of individuality.

“The whole idea behind this is multiplicity,” Johnson, who goes by he/they pronouns, said. “Native Americans and Indigenous peoples are not a single blanket. We are allowed to talk about ourselves and have ourselves seen, not as have a myth pushed onto us or woven into the American fabric.”

Among the participating artists are Kent Monkman, Onaman Collective (represented in the original posters they created for Dakota Access Pipeline protests); Anna Tsouhlarakis, who featured in the latest Whitney Biennial, contributed a banner from her Native Guide Project , that reads with the authority of Helvetica Bold: I Really Like the Way You Respect Native American Rights. The show, however, expands the notion of graphic arts beyond the boundaries drawn even by its host, Poster House. Jeffrey Gibson, who also appears in a series of jubilant collaborations with artists including Luzene Hill,Eric-Paul Riege, and Dana Claxton, is represented by a miniature ziggurat titled Because Once You Enter My House, It Becomes Our House (2020), and modeled after architecture of Cahokia, an ancient Native metropolis near modern St. Louis.

Craft, visual art, design: Where does Tony Gonyea’s ceramic wampum belt, which draws on a Haudenosaunee tradition dating to the mid-16th century, fall? And what of Ella Myers’s shadow box, Navajo Dye Chart , which, as its name suggests, displays some 40 plants and the colors they produce on wool?

“There’s a wall that is assumed, or imposed, between these categories, but someone can be a basket weaver or a rug weaver and also be engaged in graphic design. Art and design meld into everything,” Johnson said.

Read on for a conversation between Johnson and ARTnews on the show’s beginning, end, and next destination.

So, the title.

I love that the title is a double entendre: “Red” and “read.” I’m taking a racial slur and putting it right in your face, but the work is also designed to be read, understood, processed and contemplated. It’s like the Red Power movement or the American Indian Movement—taking something back that was very sacred to us and opening the entire show by punching it out.

It’s unusual to see so many three-dimensional objects in a graphic design show. What’s the thinking here?

One of the questions running through the exhibition is what counts as a poster.

For me, a poster, in a Native context, is something that communicates a message through typography, visual language or vernacular language, and is intended to be publicly shown or expressed.

Navajo Dye Chart shows how plants can be used to make different colors. The artist made posters in the 1980s, but the printing was on acidic paper and the work deteriorated quickly. There are letters still around, but I wanted the original chart—the actual object that shows where to find a particular plant and how it can be used to make a color.

That’s sovereignty: saying ‘these are the things you should be talking about.’ We don’t teach this in design history classes.

What do you make of that gap in arts and design education?

In school, we’re told that the Germans did everything, that design began with the Bauhaus, that this is how it has to be: Swiss typography. After the Bauhaus, people came to Yale, taught at Black Mountain College, and then those ideas disseminated to Cranbrook, Otis, CalArts, and other schools. Art education is stuck in the deep shadow of the Bauhaus.

[I’m a partner] at Polymode . We’ve been designing books and museum show for 20 years. In 2020, we started a school BIPOC Design History . We look at people of color who have been deliberately erased and left out of the design canon. Our school offers classes about Black design in America, Diseño Gráfico, a SWANA course, “(re)Creating Turtle Island”—we ask designers and researchers to show us what they think has been left out.

The section “Alcatraz and Protest” further complicates the distinctions between art, object, and design.

In 1969, Native Americans occupied Alcatraz Island, off San Francisco, and held it until 1971. They issued a declaration calling for the island’s return. The settlers who had occupied the island before them had left it in disrepair. Native people realized it was no longer being used and said, in effect, “We’re taking it back.” They wrote that proclamation on a piece of stretched buffalo hide.

Where did you find it?

Emma Waggoner, a graphic designer who is a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, found it. The hide was—and remains—in the collection of the U.S. Marshals Museum in Arkansas. Waggoner and her wife drove there to scout it out. They contacted the museum, though its staff was initially unsure whether they wanted to lend it to us.

I was in Santa Fe working with an archive when the archivist said, “Hang on, I know them,” and picked up the phone. He called the museum and said, “Hey, do you have this hide thing in your collection? Yeah, there’s this Native Brian Johnson who wants to get it from us.” Again, humanity is made possible by people knowing each other.

This is a key piece because it asks why Native Americans should be held to the convention of putting [design] on paper. Why would we need a huge printing press attached to the back of a horse, moving across the plains while we’re following buffalo? We can put a message on hide and put it up. And look: there’s typography and a public message, which is why this is such an important moment in the exhibition. It’s sarcastic and truthful at exactly the same time.

From the U.S. Marshals Museum—which I just learned existed—to Manhattan. How did changing the space it’s exhibited in change the object?

Here, it’s allowed to express itself, to be present and to scream. It’s not sequestered or called a prisoner; here, it has context. Is it a sacred object? No. Is it still talking to us? Yes. It’s a protest object that helped Native people gain the rights we have today.

I appreciate that Poster House cared enough to turn off the fire alarms once the show was fully installed, allowing me to sit in the institutional space. I thanked every object, especially this one, over and over. I really lived in the preparation of the room and said, “Thank you so much for being here.”

Like many pieces here, it’s attributed to ‘Designer Once Known’. In a museum, it’s more common to see on a wall text ‘Unknown artist’. What’s the nuance?

“Designer Once Known” is what we put on the label where a museum would put “Unknown.” It’s not the same thing. “Unknown” is a shrug. It’s anthropological. No way of proving it. No way of knowing. But that’s trash. The people who made that object or that work were known. They were loved. The name didn’t fall off the object. It just wasn’t valued.

“Once Known” says somebody was real, it gives them humanity again. Somebody knew whose hands cut that block, pulled that print, beaded that pennant—their name, their Nation, who taught them, their lineage, who they made it for—all the things. So when I put “Designer Once Known” on a wall, I’m not giving up on the name. I’m filing a space with dignity and the hopes of eventually one day being able to fill that in.

‘It’s Complicated’ and ‘Extractive Marketing’ are tucked in the back, a bit out of sight. What sort of work will visitors find there?

A key piece in this section was already in Poster House’s collection: a work by Winold Reiss. A German immigrant who came to the United States in the late 1880s, Reiss became an important painter during the Harlem Renaissance. He taught Aaron Douglas painting, and his portraits of Alain Locke, Langston Hughes, and Zora Neale Hurston appeared in the Met’s Harlem Renaissance exhibition.

He was also obsessed with “cowboy and Indian” stories. Went out to the Blackfeet Reservation in Montana. Got really well known there; they loved this random German guy. He paid them to sit for him, paid for a translator, painted them exactly the way they should be painted—the opposite of Edward Curtis. Painted 280 portraits. He got to know their stories and when he died, they spread his ashes on the reservation. He also sold all those paintings to the Great Northern Railroad.

And the Great Northern Railroad— ding, ding, ding —turned those portraits into marketing tools to promote its route. The company reproduced them on playing cards, business cards. None of the money went back to the reservation. Their names were not used. They were not asked for permission.

But at the same time, the typography is amazing. That’s the contradiction. The poster is beautifully made, yet it participates in a system that extracted Native people, land, and imagery for commercial gain.

It’s complicated.

It’s complicated.

Reiss ran a workshop on the reservation?

People on vacation would come to Montana and paint Native people. They were paid, but they were also treated as a bit of a sideshow, folded into the myth of the “vanishing race.” There’s something sticky about it. Why not work with them directly, or have them teach you beadwork, something from our own traditions? No, instead, it was this Michelangelo-style, grand studio. Again, the Western idea of art education.

What’s next for the show?

This is not a comprehensive show. There’s no way we could represent all 574 [federally recognized] tribes. What about the unrecognized tribes? What about the tribes that were fully erased? Which is why I’m not the only person that can speak and do this. The show needs to go somewhere like Pine Ridge, or Oklahoma City. Wherever it goes, I’d love to dig into local archives, expanding the show to fit each space. There’s a lot of Lenape material, you know, because we’re on their land. I want the people who see it to be its anchor, so it has meaning for them.

Design is fraught in many directions, as we well know, and this show has never been done before. We have to take it to underserved areas. I need Native teenagers to see that they can make these things, that they deserve to be in this space.

excerpt_original: The boundaries between craft, graphic arts, and sculpture collapse in “Designed to Be Red,” now on view at New York’s Poster House through next February.
translated_title_zh: 原创图形艺术的标志性调查将破坏预期
translated_excerpt_zh: 手工艺、图形艺术和雕塑之间的界限在“设计成为红色”中崩溃,现在在纽约的海报院展开,直到下周二。
